screens:
The session begins.

Light comes through the gaps in the shutters and lies across the floorboards in thin gold lines. Outside, Beregost is already at work. A hammer rings on an anvil, then another, then a dozen, until the whole street sounds like a smithy. A cart creaks past. Far off, Lathander's bell greets the morning.

Your purse sits on the washstand, heavy with the last hand you will ever win at cards: about three hundred and fifty gold. Your coat hangs on its peg, and your gear is where you left it. No one is waiting for you, and you owe nothing today, at least to anyone but the goddess.

From below come the smells of bacon, woodsmoke and burnt porridge. Marta Holloway, the innkeeper, is scolding someone over the clatter of plates. Under the noise you hear a softer sound you know far too well: dice rattling in a cup, then a groan, then laughter.

Penny, your cat, does not seem to care about breakfast. She sits on the sill with her nose against the shutter gap and her tail twitching slowly. She is watching something in the street below, and she has not looked away since you opened your eyes.

The day is yours. What does James do first?

Time: Day 1 · morning

James crosses the cold floorboards in his shirtsleeves. Penny allows one scratch behind the ears; her tail flicks once and her eyes stay on the street. He puts his eye to the gap beside her nose.

Through the link, as soon as he asks, comes her answer. It isn't words, just a feeling: *not food. Not a mouse. Watching.* Under it is the tight, still interest of a cat that hasn't decided whether something is a threat.

Below him the main street is full of morning. Directly across from the Anvil and Ember stands a big smithy with its yard gate wide open. A sign over the arch shows a hammer striking a cloud. A covered wagon is backed up to the gate with two grey mules in harness. A pair of men in plain brown work clothes, with no guild badges, carry pig iron out of the yard two bars at a time and stack it in the wagon bed. Judging by how low the wagon sits on its springs, they've been at it a while.

A woman in a long dust-coloured travelling coat stands by the tailboard with a ledger open on her forearm. She makes a mark for every pair of bars. Beside her, the smith wipes his hands on his apron and doesn't look happy about any of it.

A crow sits on the wagon's canvas, perfectly still.

James lets his eye settle and watches.

He watches for a good while. Mostly what he sees is a load of iron changing hands. Whatever has Penny's attention, he can't catch it. To him the crow is just a crow: black, scruffy, sitting on the canvas the way crows sit on anything. The woman's ledger is too far away to read. The smith says something to her, short and sharp, but the hammers up and down the street drown it out. She answers without looking up from her page.

When the last pair of bars goes in, she shuts the ledger, takes a fat leather purse from inside her coat and counts coins into the smith's palm. It takes a long time. The smith doesn't put the money away. He stands weighing it in his open hand, as if he's still deciding something.

On the canvas the crow hasn't moved a feather. Under James's hand, Penny's back has gone stiff, and her tail is now twitching fast.

Downstairs Marta shouts that the porridge is burning again and that it is *not her fault this time*.

 James squints through the gap until his eye waters, trying to read the scene the way Penny is reading it, and he can't. He can't find whatever she has found. The crow, the wagon, the woman and her purse all look like an ordinary morning sale to him, and the detail that has his cat bristling gets past him.

Penny gives a low, annoyed chirp, as if he's being slow. She doesn't take her eyes off the canvas.

James sets two fingers on the warm fur at the back of Penny's neck and closes his eyes. The room drops away. His own body goes dark and quiet, and he is looking out through the shutter gap with the cat's eyes.

The street changes. The morning light is sharper and flatter, and every movement stands out. The hammers are louder too, but Penny's ears pick the noise apart: a clang from the left, a hiss of quenching steel from up the road, mules shifting their hooves. Under all that, faint and in pieces, there are voices at the tailboard.

Then there's the crow.

Seen through Penny's eyes, the crow is plainly wrong. It hasn't preened, shifted its grip on the canvas or so much as glanced at the scraps in the gutter. It's facing the inn with its head cocked, and its eye is fixed on this window, on the gap where a cat's nose is pressed. It's watching Penny, the way Penny is watching it.

James knows that posture. He has seen it on his own cat, every time he rode behind her eyes the way he is doing now. That crow has someone sitting in it.

The voices come through in fragments.

"...third load this tenday," the smith says. He sounds rough and tired. "Silver over the market price on every bar. A man starts wondering, mistress."

"Then don't, Master Fuiruim," she answers, level and dry. "Wonder about something else. The price is the price."

"And if the Fist ever asks me where Beregost iron is going..."

"Tell them you sold it to a buyer who paid in full." The purse strings snap tight. "Same day next tenday. Have it ready."

The crow turns its head, just once, a quick sideways jerk toward the woman.

Without hurrying, she looks up from her purse. She doesn't glance around the street. She looks straight across it at the second floor of the Anvil and Ember, at this window, for the space of a breath. Her face is narrow and sun-browned, and nothing in it changes. Then she looks down again, tucks the ledger under her arm and says something short to her men. They climb onto the wagon bed and start lashing the canvas down. The crow doesn't move, even when the rope passes right beside it. One of the mules tosses its head and stamps, ready to go.

The smith is still in the gateway with her money in his fist, watching the wagon get ready to leave.

Under James's fingers, Penny's whole body has gone tight as a drawn bowstring. Her feeling comes through the link at the same time as the view: *it saw. It TOLD her.*

James keeps his fingers on Penny's neck and stays behind her eyes.

The labourers pull the last rope tight and climb up front. One of them clicks his tongue at the mules, and the wagon rolls out of the smithy arch with its springs groaning under the load. It doesn't turn north toward the Gate. It swings south onto the Trade Way, toward Nashkel, and joins the morning carts. The woman walks beside the front wheel for a few steps, then pulls herself up onto the bench without looking back.

The crow stays on the canvas until the wagon draws level with the inn. Then it opens its wings, beats once and rises over the street, up past the window close enough that Penny's ears go flat. It circles the roof of the Anvil and Ember once, then turns south after the wagon and stays low over the road.

James lets go. The room comes back: cold floor, the smell of porridge, his own heartbeat. Penny drops off the sill without a sound, gives herself a hard, offended shake and sits in the middle of the floor watching him dress. When he hangs the coin under his shirt, her tail gives one flick. It feels like approval.

Downstairs, Marta Holloway shouts "Breakfast's—" at his back as he walks out without stopping. Then she sighs heavily, loud enough to carry, about men who pay for porridge and don't eat it. Penny pads out after him and sits on the inn step, tucks her paws in and looks bored.

Master Fuiruim hasn't moved from the gateway. Up close he's a big, grey-bearded man with burn-scarred forearms and a leather apron shiny with wear. His fist is still closed around the money. When James speaks, the smith's eyes go to him, then to the cloak, then the coin-bulge under the shirt, the boots, and back to his face. It's how a man looks over a horse he isn't sure he wants to buy.

"Who's asking?" he says. Then, almost against his will, he glances south down the road where the dust of the wagon is settling.

James keeps his voice easy and his hands where the smith can see them. He's a stranger asking about another man's trade, but this man has plainly been wanting to tell someone all morning.

The smith is quiet for a long moment. Then he snorts through his beard, and his shoulders drop. He's been carrying this alone and is tired of it.

"You're not Fist," he says. "Fist would have come with two more and a clerk." He jerks his chin at the empty gateway. "She calls herself Mistress Orrin. First time she came was eight days ago. Didn't haggle and paid in advance, which nobody does. Three loads since. Pig iron, all of it, the best I had, and she wanted it fast. Not tools, not blades, not horseshoes. Just the raw metal."

He looks south again.

"That's what sits wrong. Nashkel's got iron mines of its own, two days nearer than here. So why does anybody haul Beregost bars south, past Nashkel's own ore, unless they don't want Nashkel knowing they're buying?" He shakes his head. "And her men. No badges, no guild. Never a word. Never stop for an ale. I've known Amnian mule-drivers who'd talk to a fencepost."

Then, slowly, he opens his fist.

Most of what's in his palm is honest money, good gold of the Gate and Amn. But four of the coins aren't. They're thicker than a gold piece and not quite round, and worn almost smooth. On one face is a bearded head, so rubbed down that only the line of a crown is left. On the other is a ring of angular letters. They look a little like dwarvish runes, but James has seen dwarvish on enough tomb doors to know they're not. Dark earth is packed hard into the grooves of the letters.

"She paid part of the first load in these too," Fuiruim says quietly. "Gold's gold, weighed out fair, so I took it. The moneychanger at the market wouldn't touch them. Said he'd never seen the mint and didn't want to." He turns one over with a thick thumb. "That's money that's been in the ground, friend. A long time."

He closes his hand again and fixes James with a hard look, narrowed and warier now.

"So. A man walks out of the Anvil and Ember without his breakfast and asks me who she's buying for. What's it to you?"

James lets the question sit for a breath before he answers. Fuiruim hears him out with his arms folded and his weight back on his heels. When James gets to the bird that never preened, the smith's eyes go past him to the inn step, where Penny is washing behind one ear and pointedly ignoring both of them.

"Rides it," Fuiruim says flatly. "Like a horse."

He looks at James a while longer, the same way he looked at him before, but slower this time. The Nashkel mines get a small grunt and nothing else; up and down the Way, everybody has buried somebody who went into those shafts. Then he looks at the open palm James is holding out. He snorts through his beard, picks one coin out of the honest gold and drops it there.

"Have your look."

It's heavy, heavier than it ought to be for its size. The edge isn't milled and isn't even round. The coin was cast, not struck: there's a faint seam where two halves of a mould met, all but worn away. James tilts it toward the morning light and runs his thumbnail along the ring of letters. He's seen a lot of old metal in his time: southern tombs, collapsed shrines in the Tethyrian hills, a dragon's leavings that turned out to be mostly brass.

It comes to him all at once, the way old things sometimes do.

He has held a coin like this before, twelve years ago in the Tethyrian hills during the war. His scout troop sheltered from the rain in a barrow, and the dead inside had these on their eyes: the same mould seam, the same heavy cast gold, the same crowned and bearded face. The old sergeant who pocketed them wouldn't spend them. He called them *under-hill gold*. He said they were older than any crown in Tethyr or Amn, left by men who learned their letters from the dwarves and later followed the dwarves into the ground. Nobody in that troop knew what became of those people. The sergeant didn't either.

Now that he's looking for it, James can see why the letters aren't dwarvish. The strokes are Dethek, cut the way a dwarf cuts them, but they don't make dwarvish words. Read as Dwarvish they're nonsense. Somebody used dwarven letters to write a language of their own.

He sees three more things the smith and the moneychanger missed.

First, the earth packed into the letters isn't forest loam or field dirt. It's grey and gritty and fine as flour, with flecks that catch the light: the rock dust that cakes a miner's boots a long way down. It's laced with rust-red that comes off on his thumbnail. This coin lay against iron for a long time, and the iron was old enough to rot.

Second, there's a mark on the reverse, inside the ring of letters, small enough to hide under a fingertip. It was punched into the metal after casting: a circle with a single straight bar through it. Whatever it is, it isn't part of the coin's design. Someone added it later, the way an assayer marks good metal or a temple marks what belongs to it. He doesn't know the sign.

Third, the coin is cold. That shouldn't matter, since it's morning and metal holds the night's chill. But he has been holding it for some time now, it hasn't warmed in his palm at all, and his hand is starting to ache faintly at the bones.

Across the street, Penny has stopped washing. She sits up on the inn step, ears forward, looking at his hand.

Fuiruim has been watching James's face, not the coin. He's seen it change.

"You know it," he says. It's not a question. "Well? And if we deal on the other three, we weigh them at Hendak's scale in the market, in front of people. I'll not have it said Fuiruim passed bad gold to a stranger at his own gate."

messages.text:
James pads to the window in his shirtsleeves, scratches Penny once behind the ears, and puts his eye to the shutter gap beside her nose to see what she's been staring at down in the street. He keeps the shutter closed and stays out of sight.

"What've you got, love? Somebody owe you money?"

James stops straining his own eye. He rests two fingers on the back of Penny's neck, closes his eyes and drops into the link, looking out through *her* eyes and listening through her ears. His attention goes to the crow on the canvas, not the coins.

"All right, clever girl. Show me."

James breathes out slowly and keeps his fingers on Penny's neck. He stays behind her eyes just long enough to see which way the wagon turns when it pulls out, north toward the Gate or south down the Way toward Nashkel. Then he lets the link go, and Penny backs away from the gap.

He steps back from the window himself, out of the light, and talks low while he pulls on his boots.

"Somebody's sitting in that bird, love, same as I sit in you. And now they know there's a cat at the Anvil and Ember with a man behind her." He buckles on the studded leather, throws the grey cloak over it and hangs Tymora's coin back under his shirt. "Fine. We'll do the open thing, then."

He leaves the purse in his pack, all but a few silver, and goes downstairs. He doesn't stop for breakfast. He heads straight across the street to the smithy gate, where Master Fuiruim is still standing with that woman's money in his fist.

James stops at a polite, unthreatening distance, nods at the hammer-and-cloud sign, and talks like a man with nothing better to do this morning.

"Morning, Master Fuiruim. That's a lot of iron going out the gate before breakfast. And by the look on your face, it's a price you're not happy to be paid." He tilts his head toward the road where the wagon went. "Who's she buying for?"

? Quick check on that roll card: it says "Persuasion +7 (Beguiling Influence)" but only added +2, so it came out 10 + 2 = 12. With the +7 from my sheet it should be 10 + 7 = 17, which beats DC 15. Was the +2 deliberate, some penalty I'm missing? Or did the card pull the wrong modifier (maybe the "skill modifier" field)? If it's a mistake, I'd like it to count as 17, a success, rather than spend one of my rerolls on it.

James lets the question sit a moment and doesn't dress it up.

"Fair question. Truth is, my cat didn't like her crow." He nods up at the inn window, where Penny now sits on the step licking a paw as if none of this concerns her. "That bird never preened once. It watched my window the whole time, and when it turned its head she looked straight up at me. Somebody was riding in it, Master Fuiruim. I know how that's done, because I do it myself." He lets that land, then shrugs. "So now she knows my face, and I'd like to know hers. That's all it is to me. That, and I've buried friends who went into the Nashkel mines and never came out, so iron going south quietly makes the back of my neck itch."

He looks at the closed fist, not greedily, just interested.

"The moneychanger won't take those four. I will, at a fair weight in good Gate gold, and you'll be shot of money you don't trust." He reaches slowly into his belt pouch for silver and gold and holds his other palm out, open. "Let me have a proper look at one first. If I know the mint, I'll tell you for nothing."

James turns the coin over once more, then sets it back in Fuiruim's palm instead of holding it. He flexes his fingers against the ache in the bones.

"I know the *kind*," he says quietly. "Not the mint. Nobody does, I think. Saw these in a barrow in the Tethyrian hills, on dead men's eyes. My old sergeant called it under-hill gold. Older than Amn, older than any crown down south. Folk who wrote with dwarf letters and then followed the dwarves into the ground." He taps the grit packed in the runes without touching the coin itself. "And that isn't field dirt. That's deep-shaft dust, and the red in it is rust off old iron. These came up out of a mine, Master Fuiruim, and not long ago."

He points at the little circle with the bar through it. "That mark was punched in after. Somebody's claimed them. You ever seen that sign on anything else? On her wagon, her ledger, a ring on her men?"

He wipes his palm on his cloak like a man brushing off frost.

"Hendak's scale is fair by me. Weighed in front of people, in good Gate gold. My purse is across the street. Give me the time it takes to climb the stairs." He holds the smith's eye a beat longer. "And a word for nothing, soldier to smith: don't keep those by your bed tonight. That one's cold, and it stays cold in a warm hand. Gold doesn't do that."

He glances over at the inn step. Penny is already on her feet.

The crow, the wagon, the woman and her purse all look like an ordinary morning sale to him, and the detail that has his cat bristling gets past him.

Penny gives a low, annoyed chirp, as if he's being slow. She doesn't take her eyes off the canvas.

turns.reply:
James sets two fingers on the warm fur at the back of Penny's neck and closes his eyes. The room drops away. His own body goes dark and quiet, and he is looking out through the shutter gap with the cat's eyes.

The street changes. The morning light is sharper and flatter, and every movement stands out. The hammers are louder too, but Penny's ears pick the noise apart: a clang from the left, a hiss of quenching steel from up the road, mules shifting their hooves. Under all that, faint and in pieces, there are voices at the tailboard.

Then there's the crow.

Seen through Penny's eyes, the crow is plainly wrong. It hasn't preened, shifted its grip on the canvas or so much as glanced at the scraps in the gutter. It's facing the inn with its head cocked, and its eye is fixed on this window, on the gap where a cat's nose is pressed. It's watching Penny, the way Penny is watching it.

James knows that posture. He has seen it on his own cat, every time he rode behind her eyes the way he is doing now. That crow has someone sitting in it.

The voices come through in fragments.

"...third load this tenday," the smith says. He sounds rough and tired. "Silver over the market price on every bar. A man starts wondering, mistress."

"Then don't, Master Fuiruim," she answers, level and dry. "Wonder about something else. The price is the price."

"And if the Fist ever asks me where Beregost iron is going..."

"Tell them you sold it to a buyer who paid in full." The purse strings snap tight. "Same day next tenday. Have it ready."

The crow turns its head, just once, a quick sideways jerk toward the woman.

Without hurrying, she looks up from her purse. She doesn't glance around the street. She looks straight across it at the second floor of the Anvil and Ember, at this window, for the space of a breath. Her face is narrow and sun-browned, and nothing in it changes. Then she looks down again, tucks the ledger under her arm and says something short to her men. They climb onto the wagon bed and start lashing the canvas down. The crow doesn't move, even when the rope passes right beside it. One of the mules tosses its head and stamps, ready to go.

The smith is still in the gateway with her money in his fist, watching the wagon get ready to leave.

Under James's fingers, Penny's whole body has gone tight as a drawn bowstring. Her feeling comes through the link at the same time as the view: *it saw. It TOLD her.*

"Morning, Master Fuiruim. That's a lot of iron going out the gate before breakfast. And by the look on your face, it's a price you're not happy to be paid." He tilts his head toward the road where the wagon went. "Who's she buying for?"

James keeps his fingers on Penny's neck and stays behind her eyes.

The labourers pull the last rope tight and climb up front. One of them clicks his tongue at the mules, and the wagon rolls out of the smithy arch with its springs groaning under the load. It doesn't turn north toward the Gate. It swings south onto the Trade Way, toward Nashkel, and joins the morning carts. The woman walks beside the front wheel for a few steps, then pulls herself up onto the bench without looking back.

The crow stays on the canvas until the wagon draws level with the inn. Then it opens its wings, beats once and rises over the street, up past the window close enough that Penny's ears go flat. It circles the roof of the Anvil and Ember once, then turns south after the wagon and stays low over the road.

James lets go. The room comes back: cold floor, the smell of porridge, his own heartbeat. Penny drops off the sill without a sound, gives herself a hard, offended shake and sits in the middle of the floor watching him dress. When he hangs the coin under his shirt, her tail gives one flick. It feels like approval.

Downstairs, Marta Holloway shouts "Breakfast's—" at his back as he walks out without stopping. Then she sighs heavily, loud enough to carry, about men who pay for porridge and don't eat it. Penny pads out after him and sits on the inn step, tucks her paws in and looks bored.

Master Fuiruim hasn't moved from the gateway. Up close he's a big, grey-bearded man with burn-scarred forearms and a leather apron shiny with wear. His fist is still closed around the money. When James speaks, the smith's eyes go to him, then to the cloak, then the coin-bulge under the shirt, the boots, and back to his face. It's how a man looks over a horse he isn't sure he wants to buy.

"Who's asking?" he says. Then, almost against his will, he glances south down the road where the dust of the wagon is settling.

James keeps his voice easy and his hands where the smith can see them. He's a stranger asking about another man's trade, but this man has plainly been wanting to tell someone all morning.

The smith is quiet for a long moment. Then he snorts through his beard, and his shoulders drop. He's been carrying this alone and is tired of it.

"You're not Fist," he says. "Fist would have come with two more and a clerk." He jerks his chin at the empty gateway. "She calls herself Mistress Orrin. First time she came was eight days ago. Didn't haggle and paid in advance, which nobody does. Three loads since. Pig iron, all of it, the best I had, and she wanted it fast. Not tools, not blades, not horseshoes. Just the raw metal."

He looks south again.

"That's what sits wrong. Nashkel's got iron mines of its own, two days nearer than here. So why does anybody haul Beregost bars south, past Nashkel's own ore, unless they don't want Nashkel knowing they're buying?" He shakes his head. "And her men. No badges, no guild. Never a word. Never stop for an ale. I've known Amnian mule-drivers who'd talk to a fencepost."

Then, slowly, he opens his fist.

Most of what's in his palm is honest money, good gold of the Gate and Amn. But four of the coins aren't. They're thicker than a gold piece and not quite round, and worn almost smooth. On one face is a bearded head, so rubbed down that only the line of a crown is left. On the other is a ring of angular letters. They look a little like dwarvish runes, but James has seen dwarvish on enough tomb doors to know they're not. Dark earth is packed hard into the grooves of the letters.

"She paid part of the first load in these too," Fuiruim says quietly. "Gold's gold, weighed out fair, so I took it. The moneychanger at the market wouldn't touch them. Said he'd never seen the mint and didn't want to." He turns one over with a thick thumb. "That's money that's been in the ground, friend. A long time."

He closes his hand again and fixes James with a hard look, narrowed and warier now.

"So. A man walks out of the Anvil and Ember without his breakfast and asks me who she's buying for. What's it to you?"

James lets the question sit a moment and doesn't dress it up.

"Fair question. Truth is, my cat didn't like her crow." He nods up at the inn window, where Penny now sits on the step licking a paw as if none of this concerns her. "That bird never preened once. It watched my window the whole time, and when it turned its head she looked straight up at me. Somebody was riding in it, Master Fuiruim. I know how that's done, because I do it myself." He lets that land, then shrugs. "So now she knows my face, and I'd like to know hers. That's all it is to me. That, and I've buried friends who went into the Nashkel mines and never came out, so iron going south quietly makes the back of my neck itch."

He looks at the closed fist, not greedily, just interested.

"The moneychanger won't take those four. I will, at a fair weight in good Gate gold, and you'll be shot of money you don't trust." He reaches slowly into his belt pouch for silver and gold and holds his other palm out, open. "Let me have a proper look at one first. If I know the mint, I'll tell you for nothing."
turns.reply:
James lets the question sit for a breath before he answers. Fuiruim hears him out with his arms folded and his weight back on his heels. When James gets to the bird that never preened, the smith's eyes go past him to the inn step, where Penny is washing behind one ear and pointedly ignoring both of them.

"Rides it," Fuiruim says flatly. "Like a horse."

He looks at James a while longer, the same way he looked at him before, but slower this time. The Nashkel mines get a small grunt and nothing else; up and down the Way, everybody has buried somebody who went into those shafts. Then he looks at the open palm James is holding out. He snorts through his beard, picks one coin out of the honest gold and drops it there.

"Have your look."

It's heavy, heavier than it ought to be for its size. The edge isn't milled and isn't even round. The coin was cast, not struck: there's a faint seam where two halves of a mould met, all but worn away. James tilts it toward the morning light and runs his thumbnail along the ring of letters. He's seen a lot of old metal in his time: southern tombs, collapsed shrines in the Tethyrian hills, a dragon's leavings that turned out to be mostly brass.

It comes to him all at once, the way old things sometimes do.

He has held a coin like this before, twelve years ago in the Tethyrian hills during the war. His scout troop sheltered from the rain in a barrow, and the dead inside had these on their eyes: the same mould seam, the same heavy cast gold, the same crowned and bearded face. The old sergeant who pocketed them wouldn't spend them. He called them *under-hill gold*. He said they were older than any crown in Tethyr or Amn, left by men who learned their letters from the dwarves and later followed the dwarves into the ground. Nobody in that troop knew what became of those people. The sergeant didn't either.

Now that he's looking for it, James can see why the letters aren't dwarvish. The strokes are Dethek, cut the way a dwarf cuts them, but they don't make dwarvish words. Read as Dwarvish they're nonsense. Somebody used dwarven letters to write a language of their own.

He sees three more things the smith and the moneychanger missed.

First, the earth packed into the letters isn't forest loam or field dirt. It's grey and gritty and fine as flour, with flecks that catch the light: the rock dust that cakes a miner's boots a long way down. It's laced with rust-red that comes off on his thumbnail. This coin lay against iron for a long time, and the iron was old enough to rot.

Second, there's a mark on the reverse, inside the ring of letters, small enough to hide under a fingertip. It was punched into the metal after casting: a circle with a single straight bar through it. Whatever it is, it isn't part of the coin's design. Someone added it later, the way an assayer marks good metal or a temple marks what belongs to it. He doesn't know the sign.

Third, the coin is cold. That shouldn't matter, since it's morning and metal holds the night's chill. But he has been holding it for some time now, it hasn't warmed in his palm at all, and his hand is starting to ache faintly at the bones.

Across the street, Penny has stopped washing. She sits up on the inn step, ears forward, looking at his hand.

Fuiruim has been watching James's face, not the coin. He's seen it change.

"You know it," he says. It's not a question. "Well? And if we deal on the other three, we weigh them at Hendak's scale in the market, in front of people. I'll not have it said Fuiruim passed bad gold to a stranger at his own gate."

---
*Out of game: earlier James took only a few silver with him and left the rest of his money in the pack upstairs at the inn, so the gold to buy the coins is across the street.*

opening.text:
Light comes through the gaps in the shutters and lies across the floorboards in thin gold lines. Outside, Beregost is already at work. A hammer rings on an anvil, then another, then a dozen, until the whole street sounds like a smithy. A cart creaks past. Far off, Lathander's bell greets the morning.

Your purse sits on the washstand, heavy with the last hand you will ever win at cards: about three hundred and fifty gold. Your coat hangs on its peg, and your gear is where you left it. No one is waiting for you, and you owe nothing today, at least to anyone but the goddess.

From below come the smells of bacon, woodsmoke and burnt porridge. Marta Holloway, the innkeeper, is scolding someone over the clatter of plates. Under the noise you hear a softer sound you know far too well: dice rattling in a cup, then a groan, then laughter.

Penny, your cat, does not seem to care about breakfast. She sits on the sill with her nose against the shutter gap and her tail twitching slowly. She is watching something in the street below, and she has not looked away since you opened your eyes.

The day is yours. What does James do first?

epilogue.text:
Epilogue — the table closed on 25 October 2026 after 5 turns

Master Fuiruim stood in his gateway long enough for a man to climb the stairs of the Anvil and Ember and come back down. Then he stood a while longer. Across the street the cat had already left the step. By the time the hammers broke for the noon meal, the smith had stopped watching the inn door. He went back to his forge with the honest gold in one pocket and the four cold coins in the other.

He did not keep them by his bed. He would not say whose advice that had been. That evening he banked his fire high, put the four coins in a crucible and watched them slump into one bright puddle. The seam of the mould went, then the crowned head, then the letters that were not dwarvish, then the little barred circle. The grey grit burned off as a thin, sour smoke and was gone. What cooled in the ingot mould was gold, and nothing more. It warmed in his hand like any metal.

Hendak weighed it at his scale in the market, in front of people, as Fuiruim wanted. He paid a fair rate for plain melt and asked no questions, since melt has no mint to worry about. Fuiruim spent it on charcoal and a new apron. He never spoke of it again, except once to say that the stranger had owed him nothing in the end, and that this was its own kind of fair.

Mistress Orrin's wagon came on the appointed day the following tenday. The iron was ready, and she paid in good Amnian gold with nothing old among it. She marked her ledger, said nothing about any window, and turned south. No crow sat on the canvas. She did not come the tenday after, or any tenday after that. Her silent men went with her, and no one in Beregost ever learned their names. The Flaming Fist never came asking where the iron had gone, so Fuiruim never had to tell them.

A season on, Beregost sounds the way it always has. The hammers start before dawn, Lathander's bell answers them, and the carts groan up and down the Way. The smithy under the hammer-and-cloud sells horseshoes and hinges and the occasional blade. Fuiruim prices his pig iron at the market rate again. In the market, Hendak's scale still settles every argument it is brought.

Nashkel works its own mines and sends its own ore north and south. The talk in its taverns is of cave-ins and wages and weather, the same talk as every year. If three wagonloads of Beregost bars passed through on their way somewhere, no one there remembers them.

At the Anvil and Ember, Marta Holloway still burns the porridge and still insists it is not her fault. The room with the shuttered window has been let a dozen times since. Its light still lies across the floorboards in thin gold lines. Now and then, out of habit, she sets out a dish of scraps on the step for a cat that does not come.

James Worgen went out of Beregost the way such men go, with his purse on his shoulder, his coin under his shirt and his grey cat at his heel. He owed nothing to anyone but the goddess. He was in the town for one morning, he asked one honest question, and then he was not there. The town did not remark on it. It closed around the place where he had stood, the way water closes over a dropped coin, and it went on ringing.
